body.text: The annual UN climate change negotiations, whose latest instalment, COP31, kicks off this week in the Turkish coastal resort of Antalya — with, somewhat bizarrely, Australia in the chair — is always a good time to take stock of where the world has got to on this most attention-grabbing yet apparently ignorable of global issues. Are we still going to hell in a handbasket, or is there yet hope of getting out of the handbasket just before Satan opens the gates?
The answer is yes and yes. This is the paradox at the heart of global warming: the situation is both worse and better than you thought.

Let’s start with the bad news. The rate at which the planet is heating up is accelerating. From 1975 to 2015 the Earth’s average surface temperatures rose at a rate of around 0.2C per decade. But the last ten years have seen warming of 0.35C. This is despite the fact that the growth of greenhouse gas emissions over that period has slowed dramatically.

What is going on? Unfortunately, warming creates positive feedback effects, and these are now speeding the process up. As the planet’s ice and snow cover decline with higher temperatures, less solar radiation is reflected back out of the atmosphere. At the same time warming is generating new types of cloud formation that are better at trapping heat and worse at reflecting it. As a result, the Earth’s “reflectivity” is declining. As it absorbs more solar radiation, the atmosphere heats up more quickly. Even our successes are part of the problem: global environmental policies have removed some important reflecting particles, such as sulphates, from the atmosphere.

This means that, contrary to what we might have expected as global emissions level off, the temperature limits set by the United Nations in the 2015 Paris climate agreement are going to be hit earlier than previously thought. The Paris agreement seeks to limit warming to “well below” 2C (relative to pre-industrial temperatures) and if possible no more than 1.5C. We are already at 1.4C, with 2024 by far the hottest year on record and 2026 likely to match it. The ten-year average is expected to exceed 1.5C in 2030, and 2C now looks likely before 2050. On governments’ current emissions reduction plans, warming will continue for the rest of the century, reaching around 2.6C above pre-industrial levels.

Over the past year most parts of the world have experienced one or more of the extreme events associated with 1.4C of warming: deadly heatwaves, uncontrollable wildfires, catastrophic hurricanes, typhoons, droughts and floods. As temperatures continue to rise, all of these will become more frequent and more severe, and extend further north and south of the equator. Above 1.8C the rise in sea levels will accelerate, fragile ecosystems such as coral reef ecosystems will collapse, and there will be a profound melting of the “cryosphere” — the planet’s ice sheets, sea ice, glaciers, permafrost and snow.

And at an unknown time after that point, something else may happen as well, for climate change is not linear. We may hit tipping points in critical global systems such as the West Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets, the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, and the Amazon rainforest. Rather than changing gradually, these would see sudden and irreversible shifts in their states. Each would have a profound effect on climatic patterns: a recent report by the UN Environment Programme baldly noted that such changes would “reshape the world forever.”

It is important to recognise that the Paris goal of limiting warming to 2C is still within reach. Indeed, so is an end goal of 1.5C, though only (after exceeding it) by returning to it from a peak of 1.8C. In September the UN Environment Programme gave such an “overshoot” trajectory its official sanction as the best now available. But it also noted that achieving it will require two significant changes to governments’ current plans.

The first is that countries will have to speed up their emissions reductions by weaning themselves off fossil fuels faster than presently envisaged. The current projection is that the world will reach net zero emissions around 2070; that won’t be soon enough. The second is that they must start investing in global cooling.

Active planetary cooling can be done in two main ways. One is through carbon dioxide removal, or CDR, the process of taking greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere. Some of this occurs naturally, in photosynthesis by plants. Many governments already include in their climate mitigation plans measures to capture and store more carbon through afforestation, ecosystem restoration and better soil management. They will need to do more of it.

But UNEP warns that this will not be enough. Such is the rate of global heating that novel methods of carbon removal will also be required. These include accelerating the creation of carbonates from rock weathering; the fertilisation of phytoplankton in the ocean by adding iron; and “direct air capture,” in which CO2 is sucked out of the atmosphere by high-tech machines. All these methods are now being piloted, but they remain expensive, some of them raise obvious environmental risks, and none of them yet have in place agreed mechanisms to govern their use.

UNEP nevertheless insists they must be on the agenda. If the best hope for the world now is to overshoot 1.5C and then return to it, that will mean not just cutting emissions to slow the rise in temperature but also expanding removals; and then using removals to achieve “net negative emissions” to cool the planet back down again.

But other scientists note that even this will not be sufficient. Because temperatures are rising so fast, they are demanding governments consider the second means of active cooling. This is increasing the Earth’s reflectivity to prevent heat reaching the Earth in the first place. Various methods are available to do this. Some, such as limiting aircraft contrails (which trap heat) and expanding the Earth’s white surface areas, both of buildings and crops, are relatively uncontroversial. But increasingly urgent calls are also now being heard for “solar radiation management,” such as adding salts to and thereby brightening marine clouds, or injecting aerosols into the stratosphere.

Such “geoengineering” techniques have been widely rejected by environmental NGOs and others, usually citing concerns about uncontrolled environmental impacts and the lack of an international framework for their governance. It is feared that such methods will distract countries and companies from the urgent present task of emissions reduction. So far a limited amount of research is being done in a few countries, but no government has yet brought the topic to the negotiating table.

If the science looks bleak, what then is the source of climate optimism? It lies in the progress being made towards cheap emissions reduction. Over the past few years the world has embarked on a remarkable shift from using fossil fuels for heating and transport to using electricity, and from using fossil fuels to generate electricity to using renewables. And it is making this shift not, primarily, because of climate change, but for three much more politically urgent reasons: because fossil fuels are choking the world’s city dwellers to death (air pollutants are estimated to kill eight million people a year), they have become more expensive than renewables, and (as the wars in Ukraine and Iran have proved) they are a less reliable energy source.

In 2025 global investment in the “clean energy transition” (defined as including renewables, nuclear, carbon capture, hydrogen, energy storage, electrified heat, electric vehicles, clean industry, clean shipping and power grids) reached US$2.3 trillion, up 8 per cent over the previous year and more than double the level of five years before. As might be expected, China accounted for around a third of the global total (US$800 billion); but even the otherwise economically struggling European Union saw growth of 18 per cent (to US$455 billion). Perhaps most remarkably, Donald Trump’s concerted attempts to slow the transition in the US could not prevent a 3.5 per cent increase (to US$378 billion).

More money is now invested globally in clean energy supply than in the supply of fossil fuels; the latter is actually falling. The largest single area of investment is in electric vehicles and associated charging infrastructure (US$893 billion), up more than a fifth on the previous year. One in four new cars bought last year was electric.

The global shift to clean energy is rapid, though not yet rapid enough to slow the rise in global temperature. But it could do so. The Energy Transitions Commission, an international coalition of energy experts, companies and financial institutions, has just published a helpful report showing what would be required to hold warming to 1.8C before any subsequent return to 1.5C. Five methods will be needed, they argue: accelerating the electrification of the global economy; running down existing coal generation faster than currently planned; decarbonising sectors that are “hard to electrify” (heavy industry, aviation and shipping) by mid-century; cutting annual methane emissions by around half by 2050; and stopping deforestation by 2035.

Electrification makes the single largest contribution to the plan. And, critically, it could be done at more or less zero economic cost. (All the others would represent net costs, though stopping deforestation would obviously have huge ecological co-benefits.) This is because electric vehicles are already, on a lifetime basis, cheaper than the petrol and diesel models they are replacing; and electric heating is rapidly becoming cheaper than gas. Most of all, it is because of the rapidly declining cost and rapidly improving performance of battery storage. Lithium-ion batteries now cost just a tenth of what they did in 2010, while at the utility scale needed for power generation, battery storage costs have fallen by 60 per cent in the past five years.

This is why electrification has become the new watchword, not just for climate advocates but for the entire energy industry. A new global coalition of governments, business groups and civil society organisations, was launched in June called Electrify Now. At Davos this year the head of the International Energy Agency, Fatih Birol, had a simple message for the assembled world leaders: “electrify everything.”

So the planet is warming more quickly than before but cost-effective technological options exist to cut emissions more rapidly. Presumably all this is what the COP31 negotiators will be discussing in Turkey?

Er, no. The official agenda includes nothing on the latest climate science and the need for novel means of carbon dioxide removal or other cooling methods. There is no place for talks on how to close the “emissions gap” between current plans and the overshoot trajectory to 1.5C, or on accelerating electrification. The main focus of the negotiations will be, as it often is, on how developed countries can scale up their financial assistance to the poorest and most vulnerable developing countries.

Though it’s not quite true that there will be no discussion of electrification. Following the trend of recent conferences, COP31 will have two separate parts. There will be the formal negotiations conducted by official negotiators trying to achieve consensus among 197 governments on predefined texts. And then there will be the non-negotiated “Action Agenda,” a series of side events, declarations and “coalitions of the willing” where governments, businesses and financial institutions will seek to make progress in the real world of energy, industry, methane emissions, deforestation, nature recovery and other topics.

In last year’s unseemly scrap between Australia and Turkey to host COP31 — a spectacle not a few observers described as a fine case of bald men fighting over a comb — it was Australia’s energy minister Chris Bowen who got the task of hosting the negotiations, while Turkey not only got a boost to its tourist industry but was given charge of the Action Agenda. And it wasted little time in making the most of it. Supported by Australia, it declared its intention to achieve agreement on a new “35 by 35” electrification target: that electricity’s share of global energy consumption should be increased from its current 23 per cent to 35 per cent by 2035.

The Action Agenda target joins a range of other initiatives launched at COPs but not actually agreed by them. Last year Brazil, host of COP30, sought to overcome the conference’s failure to agree the production of “roadmaps” on deforestation and clean energy by promising that it would produce these itself. It published them last week. One sets out how the world can “transition away from fossil fuels” while boosting economic growth and reducing poverty; it picks up on the joint Netherlands–Colombia conference earlier this year in which sixty countries pledged to produce national roadmaps of their own.

The other roadmap produced by Brazil analyses how sustainable forest management can provide long-term export industries for host countries alongside better livelihoods for forest peoples. The re-election of President Lula has given the global prospects for halting deforestation a huge shot in the arm: since he became president again in 2022 deforestation in Brazil has fallen by more than 70 per cent to its lowest level since records began in 1988. Indonesia will bring to COP a new pledge that it will stop clearing land for what would have been the largest deforestation project in the world.

These are interesting developments, because they are beginning to bridge the gap between the formal negotiations at COPs and the non-formal Action Agenda. In terms of international law and UN process, the Action Agenda has no status. But as the formal negotiations struggle for relevance in years when new goals and targets are not up for discussion, the Action Agenda is increasingly, well, where the action is. It is notable that the UN Secretariat has set up an official portal where countries can submit their own fossil fuel transition plans. And Turkey and Australia are seeking to get the 35 by 35 electrification goal agreed, not just on the informal stage, but in the official COP31 final text itself.

They are likely to succeed, because a goal for the whole world does not commit any individual country to do anything. The “axis of obstruction” that prevented progress on fossil fuels last year — Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Russia and their allies — will not stand in the way of a global goal that doesn’t mention, or even technically imply, any reduction in demand for fossil fuels. But it will nevertheless be a significant moment: a commitment promoted through the informal COP process forcing its way into the formal one. Who knows, next year COP32 might even discuss the need for global cooling. •
